description:
Interested in all kinds of sciences, background in AI, coding, data analysis, space physics, maths and world agriculture and world commodity trading. 

Planning to build a tool that could change the world, that could really be useful. 

Planning on resolving farmer-struggles, with the help of science, for the sake of science.
summary: Soil Futures is a free web app that helps a smallholder farmer decide what to grow on one field over the next ten years. The farmer pins their field on a map, says what they grow and can add a quick spade-and-hand soil check. Soil Futures combines 35 years of NASA POWER weather, MODIS satellite greenness, SMAP soil moisture and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate projections with global soil maps. It simulates every crop day by day across 25 replayed weather years and ranks five crop rotations by crop–climate fit, soil health, water, income, labour and weather risk. The farmer gets plain answers (what to sow next and when, what to watch out for, what the plan does to the soil), a 10-year timeline, week-by-week season calendars, a 3D view of the field and its soil, a field risk map and a budget. Every number shows its source and a likely range. It works in seven languages on low-cost phones. Soil degradation and a changing climate hit hardest the farmers with the least access to agronomic advice; Soil Futures puts NASA's Earth observations in their hands.
details:
What it does

Soil Futures turns NASA Earth observations into a ten-year crop plan for one field. A farmer marks the field on a map (place search, GPS or a tap), says what grows there now and what grew before, whether it is irrigated and whether trees grow on it, and sets five priorities: soil health, water savings, income, labour and risk tolerance. An optional soil check asks what a spade and a hand can tell (texture by feel, crusting, drainage, slope, depth, hard layers) and accepts lab results.

How it works

- Weather: 35 years of daily NASA POWER data for the field. Past years are adjusted to today's climate and replayed as 25 possible futures; later years carry the climate change projected by NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 (three models, SSP2-4.5).

- Crop model: each crop is simulated day by day: growth stages from degree-days, water use from the FAO-56 method, yield from intercepted sunlight, losses from drought, heat at flowering, frost, waterlogging, salt and disease.

- Soil bank: a weekly "bank account" for soil health. Living roots, residue and legumes are deposits; bare soil, tillage and repeating the same crop are withdrawals.

- Optimizer: a genetic search compares hundreds of rotations, with cover crops and trees, scheduled on the field's real calendar, and ranks the best five for the farmer's priorities, each with the reasons behind it.

- Season calendar: the best sowing window, growth stages, harvest window and alerts (heat, drought, frost, wet harvest), week by week.

- 360° field view: a 3D block of the field that replays a season day by day in a poor, typical and good year, above and below ground.

- Field risks and trends: where on the field erosion, water stress, frost and heat are worst, from terrain and weather, how that changed since 1991, and "what if" climate scenarios.

- Farm records: seasons, observations and harvests, yield forecasts with ranges, and a budget that spreads the money the farmer can spend over the plan. Farms that agree share pseudonymized records so forecasts improve for everyone.

- Data files: farmers can add their own data (spreadsheets, GeoTIFF, NetCDF, shapefiles…); other public sources (ESA Sentinel-2, ERA5-Land, FAO GAEZ, and USDA soil and crop maps in the US) are read for each field.

-Learning from all farms (Supabase): Farms that agree to share send pseudonymised records to a shared PostgreSQL database on Supabase (hosted in the EU): seasons, harvests, weather, forecasts and their outcomes. No names, notes or exact locations are sent, only a 0.5° climate cell and a country, and money spent is never shared. Every 24 hours the server retrains a model on these records. It learns how each region's real harvests differ from what the crop model expects, then uses ridge regression on weather, inputs, soil and timing, tested with 5-fold cross-validation grouped by farm. A new model replaces the current one only if it predicts at least 5% better, and only once 150 seasons from 20 farms are available. Until then, forecasts use FAOSTAT country yields and regional averages. Results are shown only when at least 3 farms stand behind them. Simulated farmers are used to test the learning but never train the live model, and a farmer who opts out has their records deleted.

Benefits and intended impact

Smallholders rarely get field-specific advice. Soil Futures gives it for free, in plain words, in seven languages (English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Hindi, Chinese, Indonesian), on low-cost phones and slow connections. It favours plans that build soil and spread risk, so farmers can earn today without degrading the land they depend on.

Honesty and safety by design

Every number shows its source and whether it is observed, estimated or projected, and every prediction shows a range. When a source is unavailable, the fallback is labelled. The app never gives fertilizer, lime or pesticide rates (it points to a lab test and local advice), and it never claims certainty about yields, prices or weather. Only the field's location rounded to about 100 m leaves the device; there is no advertising or tracking.

Tools

JavaScript on Node.js (no external packages), HTML and CSS, Web Workers, Leaflet maps, three.js for 3D, PostgreSQL on Supabase for the shared learning data, and 151 automated tests. AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic, through Claude Code) was used for making the demo video, as well as for finding good external sources and resources, and ElevenLabs generated the demo's voice-over.

Limits we state openly

NASA POWER weather describes a ~50 km cell, not the field itself; the soil bank is rule-based; the crop model is not calibrated to each farm; and some sources (SMAP and ECOSTRESS via AppEEARS) need a NASA Earthdata login.
